title: Requirements & Malfunctions
description: What an aircraft engine must do and how to read its data, and how its common malfunctions show themselves and are found: detonation, pre-ignition, backfiring, afterfiring, blow-by and the run-up checks.

lessons.title: Engine Requirements
lessons.objective: Summarise what an aircraft piston engine must deliver (power for its weight, economy, durability and reliability, flexibility, compactness), say how engines are chosen, and read the leading particulars of the GTSIO-520-H from its manual.
lessons.completionCriteria: State the general requirements of an aircraft engine, calculate specific weight and brake-specific fuel consumption, and find and interpret the leading particulars on an engine data sheet, including the condition each figure is quoted for.

steps.title: What an engine must do
steps.prompt: Think of an engine for a small training aircraft and one for a long-range airliner. What do both owners want? Write down five things before you read on. The handbook lists the general requirements every aircraft engine must meet: efficiency, economy and reliability, a low weight for its power, sustained high power without losing reliability, a long time between overhauls, compactness with easy access for maintenance, as little vibration as possible, and a wide range of power at different speeds and altitudes.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 22-23 (all aircraft engines must meet general requirements of efficiency, economy and reliability; economical in procurement, fuel and maintenance; low weight-to-horsepower ratio; sustained high power output without sacrificing reliability; durable between overhauls; compact yet accessible; as vibration free as possible; a wide range of power at various speeds and altitudes). The course deck (slides 202-205) groups them as power and weight, fuel economy, durability and reliability, operating flexibility, compactness and powerplant selection.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt that lets the learner meet the list before it is organised.

steps.title: Power and weight
steps.prompt: Every extra pound an engine carries lowers the aircraft's performance, so engines are judged by their specific weight, the weight per brake horsepower. Lower is better: it raises the useful load. Take the GTSIO-520-H, which develops 375 horsepower and has a standard dry weight of 550.39 lb. Its specific weight is 550.39 ÷ 375 = 1.47 lb per horsepower. Better design and better metals have brought the specific weight of reciprocating engines down a great deal.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 23 (the weight of an engine per brake horsepower is its specific weight; decreasing it increases the useful load and the performance; improved design and metallurgy have improved the power-to-weight ratio of reciprocating engines) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152-153 (375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm; standard engine dry weight 550.39 lb). The result is a worked example from those two numbers.

mediaPlan.rationale: A definition with a worked number from the course engine.

steps.title: Fuel economy
steps.prompt: Fuel economy is measured as specific fuel consumption. For a reciprocating engine it is the fuel flow in pounds per hour divided by the brake horsepower, called brake-specific fuel consumption. An engine that burns 150 lb of fuel an hour while developing 300 brake horsepower has a brake-specific fuel consumption of 0.5 lb per hour per brake horsepower. The lower the figure, the better the economy. At low speed reciprocating and turboprop engines are more economical than turbojets and turbofans; at high speed, losses in the propeller limit them.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 23 (the basic parameter for fuel economy is specific fuel consumption; for reciprocating engines the fuel flow in lb/hr divided by brake horsepower, called brake-specific fuel consumption; reciprocating and turboprop engines have better economy at low speed, and above 400 mph propeller losses limit them) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 44 (Figure 2-2, specific fuel consumption). The 150 lb/hr and 300 bhp numbers are invented for the example.

mediaPlan.rationale: A definition with a short invented example, so the formula is used once.

steps.title: Durability and reliability
steps.prompt: Reliability and durability go together but are not the same. Reliability is how often the engine fails, measured as the mean time between failures: a reliable engine performs at its rated power in any flight attitude and in extreme weather. Durability is how long the engine lasts while it stays reliable, measured as the mean time between overhauls, the TBO. The manufacturer builds both in by design and test, and recommends a TBO. No fixed TBO is guaranteed, because it depends on temperatures, time at high power and the maintenance given. After that, keeping the engine reliable is up to the people who maintain, overhaul and operate it.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 23-24 (reliability measured as mean time between failures and durability as mean time between overhauls; reliability means performing at the specified ratings in varying flight attitudes and extreme weather; no definite TBO is specified or implied by the rating, and it varies with operating conditions, time at high power and maintenance; recommended TBOs are specified by the engine manufacturer; continued reliability is determined by maintenance, overhaul and operating personnel).

mediaPlan.rationale: Two definitions and a caution that are best stated side by side.

steps.title: Flexible and compact
steps.prompt: Operating flexibility is the ability to run smoothly and give the performance wanted at every speed from idle to full power, and in the full range of atmospheric conditions. Compactness matters for three reasons. A smaller, well-shaped engine streamlines and balances the aircraft better, it gives the pilot of a single-engine aircraft a better view, and it creates less drag. Weight and compactness are linked: the longer and more spread out an engine is, the harder it is to keep its specific weight down.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24 (operating flexibility; compactness for streamlining and balancing, pilot view and drag; weight limitations are closely related to compactness).

mediaPlan.rationale: Two short requirements that read best together.

steps.title: Choosing an engine
steps.prompt: No single engine is best everywhere, so the choice depends on the mission. The handbook gives a guide by cruising speed. Up to about 250 mph the reciprocating engine is the usual choice, for its efficiency and low cost, and a turbosupercharged one holds its rated power to high altitude. From about 180 to 350 mph the turboprop does very well, because it gives more power per pound. From 350 mph up to Mach 0.8 to 0.9, turbofans are generally used by airlines, and above that, turbojets and low-bypass turbofans. Gas turbines are most economical at high altitude, but cost limits their use.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24 (powerplant selection: reciprocating engines for aircraft whose cruising speed does not exceed 250 mph; turbosupercharged reciprocating engines for high altitude performance; turboprops perform very well from 180 to 350 mph; turbofans from 350 mph to Mach 0.8-0.9; Mach 1 and above by turbojets, afterburning and low-bypass turbofans; the cost of gas turbines is a limiting factor).

mediaPlan.rationale: A selection guide by speed band, stated once and tested in the checks.

steps.title: The data plate and the engine's name
steps.prompt: Every certified engine carries a permanent, fireproof data plate that identifies it, with at least its maker, its model and its serial number. The serial number lets you track its total time, time since overhaul and any airworthiness directives. The model name is a code. In GTSIO-520-H the manual's general information says the engine is geared (G), turbocharged (T), fuel injected (I) and horizontally opposed (O), and 520 is its displacement in cubic inches. The H marks the variant, and a limit that belongs to another variant does not apply.
steps.note: The regulatory content of the data plate (14 CFR 45.13 and EASA Part 21) and the use of the serial number are from the course deck (slide 207); the handbook pages read here do not describe the engine data plate, so the instructor should confirm the wording against the regulation. The engine's description is from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (C-3-2: geared, turbocharged, six-cylinder, fuel injected, horizontally opposed, 520 cubic inches). The deck reads the letters as G for geared, TS for turbosupercharged, I for fuel injected and O for opposed.

mediaPlan.rationale: The naming rule is the content; the next steps show the real data.

steps.title: Leading particulars
steps.prompt: Here is the first page of the GTSIO-520-H's detail specifications from its overhaul manual. Find these: the power it develops and at what propeller speed; the propeller drive ratio; the bore, stroke and displacement; the compression ratio; the fuel grade; and the drive ratios of the magnetos, the tachometer and the starter. The numbers are the engine's leading particulars.
steps.alt: GTSIO-520-H general information and detail engine specifications, page C-3-2: it is geared, turbocharged, six-cylinder, fuel injected and horizontally opposed, and develops 375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm; propeller drive ratio 0.667:1; bore 5.250 in; stroke 4.000 in; displacement 520 cu in; compression ratio 7.5:1; turbosupercharger maximum 75,000 rpm; oil sump 13 quarts; fuel 100LL or 100; magneto drive 1.5:1; tachometer 0.5:1; starter drive 32:1.
steps.credit: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, page C-3-2
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (page C-3-2, general information and detail engine specifications for the GTSIO-520-H). Teaching extract of a manufacturer manual dated June 1980; always use the current data for the engine in front of you.

mediaPlan.rationale: The manufacturer's own specification page is the real "leading particulars" the module asks the learner to identify.

steps.title: Operating particulars
steps.prompt: The second page continues with the other drive ratios, the spark timing and plug gap, the firing order, the fuel pressures, and the limits for oil pressure, oil temperature and cylinder head temperature. It ends with the dry weight. Find the spark timing, the firing order, the maximum cylinder head temperature and the normal and maximum oil temperature.
steps.alt: GTSIO-520-H detail engine specifications, continued, page C-3-3: alternator drive 3:1; vacuum pump drive 1.14:1; propeller governor drive 0.809:1; spark 20 degrees before top centre on both magnetos; spark plug gap 0.017 to 0.018 in; firing order 1-4-5-2-3-6; unmetered fuel pressure 6.0 psi at 450 propeller rpm; maximum metered fuel pressure 16.0 to 17.0 psi at 39.5 inches of mercury manifold pressure and 2275 propeller rpm; oil pressure 100 psi maximum and 10 psi minimum at idle; oil temperature 170 normal and 240 maximum degrees Fahrenheit; cylinder head temperature 460 maximum and 200 minimum for takeoff; standard dry weight 550.39 lb.
steps.credit: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, page C-3-3
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 153 (page C-3-3, detail engine specifications continued; dated June 1980). The limits are for teaching reading of a data sheet and are not an operating instruction.

mediaPlan.rationale: The second page of the manufacturer specification gives the timing, firing order and limits.

steps.title: Reading the numbers
steps.prompt: The data are linked, so you can check them against each other. The 0.667:1 propeller drive means the propeller turns at 0.667 of the crankshaft speed, so at 2275 propeller rpm the crankshaft is turning at 2275 ÷ 0.667 = about 3,411 rpm: the engine runs fast, and the reduction gear slows the propeller. A six-cylinder four-stroke engine fires six times in two turns, which is once every 720° ÷ 6 = 120° of the crankshaft, in the order 1-4-5-2-3-6. Fuel pressure is quoted at a stated manifold pressure and propeller speed, 39.5 inches of mercury and 2275 rpm. A number is only meaningful with its conditions.
steps.note: Calculations from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152-153 (propeller drive ratio 0.667:1; 375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm; firing order 1-4-5-2-3-6; maximum metered fuel pressure at 39.5 inches of mercury manifold pressure and 2275 propeller rpm) and the 720° cycle from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The firing order also appears in the FAA handbook as the usual six-cylinder opposed order (PDF p. 37).

mediaPlan.rationale: Worked checks that the learner can repeat on the manual page.

steps.title: Read an engine data sheet
steps.prompt: You are handed the data sheet of an engine you have not seen before. In your own words: which numbers describe its size and power, which describe its drives, which are limits and what is the condition each is quoted for, and which of the general requirements (power and weight, fuel economy, durability and reliability, flexibility, compactness) can you judge from it and which can you not? Then take the lesson's quiz.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the requirements to a data sheet (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 22-24, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 152-153.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner works with a data sheet in their own words.

lessons.title: Operation Malfunctions
lessons.objective: Outline detonation, pre-ignition, backfiring, afterfiring and blow-by: say what each is, what causes it, how it shows itself, and use the magneto check, the power check and the cold cylinder check to find the cylinder at fault.
lessons.completionCriteria: Define detonation, pre-ignition, backfiring, afterfiring and blow-by and tell them apart, state the usual cause and the first action for each, interpret a fast or slow magneto drop, and read a set of cold cylinder readings to name the dead cylinder.

steps.title: What normal combustion looks like
steps.prompt: Before you can tell what is wrong, know what is right. In a healthy cylinder the spark starts a flame that spreads across the chamber in ripples from each plug, at about 100 feet a second, and the pressure rises at a steady rate to a peak just after the piston has passed top dead centre. That is the moment the push on the piston is best used. Every malfunction in this lesson is combustion that departs from that pattern. As you read about each one, ask three questions: when does the burning start, how fast does it go, and where does it happen?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 397 (normal combustion: the mixture ignites and burns progressively at a fairly uniform rate; with correct timing the maximum pressure builds just after the piston passes top dead centre; flame fronts start at each plug and burn in wavelike forms; flame travel is about 100 feet per second, influenced by the fuel, the air-fuel ratio, and the pressure and temperature of the mixture). The three questions are this lesson's framing.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction frame that sets the learner up to compare each fault with the normal pattern.

steps.title: Normal combustion and detonation
steps.prompt: On the left, normal combustion: the flame spreads outward from the plug in rings, and the piston feels a firm, even push. On the right, detonation: the last part of the charge explodes by itself, and the piston feels a hammer blow. Notice where the burst starts. It is not at the plug.
steps.alt: FAA figure of two cylinders. On the left, normal combustion: concentric rings of flame spread outward from the spark plug and a hand pushes the piston down firmly. On the right, detonation: an explosion in the far side of the chamber and a fist hammering the piston.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 397 (Figure 10-42, normal combustion within a cylinder, and Figure 10-43, detonation within a cylinder).

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook's paired figure shows the difference between the two kinds of burning in one glance.

steps.title: Detonation
steps.prompt: Every fuel has a limit of temperature and compression. Beyond it, the fuel ignites by itself. Detonation is the spontaneous burning of the unburned charge ahead of the flame fronts after the spark. The flame fronts squeeze the gas ahead of them while the rising piston squeezes it too; if the total compression on the last gas to burn passes the critical point, it explodes. The result is a violent pressure rise, great heat and turbulence that scrub the cylinder and piston, and the handbook warns it can burn a hole completely through the piston. A low-octane fuel in an engine that needs high octane is the standard example.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 397 (all fuels have critical limits of temperature and compression; detonation is the spontaneous combustion of the unburned charge ahead of the flame fronts after ignition; the explosive burning produces an extremely rapid pressure rise and a scrubbing action that can burn a hole completely through the piston) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 44 (detonation occurs when the charge meets a temperature and pressure above the safe limit of the fuel; low-octane fuel in an engine that requires high octane is an example).

mediaPlan.rationale: The figure on the previous step carries the picture; this step gives the definition and the cause.

steps.title: Why detonation hides
steps.prompt: Light to medium detonation causes no roughness, no temperature rise and no loss of power, so it can go on through every takeoff without the crew knowing. Often it is found only when the engine is torn down: dished piston heads, collapsed valve heads, broken ring lands, or eroded valves, pistons and cylinder heads. So prevention matters more than detection. The design supplies rich mixtures at high power, because a rich mixture does not detonate as readily as a lean one. The rest is up to the crew and the technician: respect the rpm and manifold pressure limits, use the right fuel grade and mixture, and keep cylinder head and carburettor air temperatures down. Timing that is too early can also cause it.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 397-398 (at high power the mixture is made richer because a rich mixture does not detonate as readily; light to medium detonation gives no flight deck evidence; severe detonation is found at overhaul as dished piston heads, collapsed valve heads, broken ring lands, or eroded valves, pistons or heads; the basic protection is the design, the rating limits and the correct grade of fuel; the ground and flight crews must observe rpm and manifold pressure limits and use the supercharger, mixture and temperatures correctly) and PDF p. 396 (early ignition can cause detonation and loss of power at takeoff power settings). The course deck (slide 252) lists detonation damage as a reason for disassembly: piston erosion, valve burning and cylinder head cracking. The 2025-2026 daily quiz activity asks that excessively advanced ignition timing can result in detonation, structural damage and potential engine failure.

mediaPlan.rationale: Text and consequences only; the learner has the figure from the previous step.

steps.title: Pre-ignition
steps.prompt: Pre-ignition means the charge starts to burn before the timed spark jumps. The cause is a hot spot: a deposit of carbon or lead glowing in the chamber, a cracked valve or piston, or a broken spark plug insulator acting as a glow plug. Detonation often leads to it, because the roughened, eroded surface it leaves behind glows. High power on a very lean mixture can also cause it. The signs in the flight deck are engine roughness, backfiring and a sudden rise in cylinder head temperature. The remedy is to cool the cylinder: retard the throttle, lower the manifold pressure if you can, and enrich the mixture.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 398 (pre-ignition is combustion before the timed spark; it is often traced to carbon or other deposits that cause hot spots; detonation often leads to it, and high-power operation on excessively lean mixtures may also cause it; indicated by engine roughness, backfiring and a sudden increase in cylinder head temperature; any incandescent area serves as an igniter; a cracked valve or piston or a broken spark plug insulator may furnish a hot point; the immediate step is to retard the throttle, reduce manifold pressure if a supercharger is in use, and then enrich the mixture) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 44 (pre-ignition when the charge ignites before the normal ignition event; a leaking valve can overheat until its edge is incandescent). The EASA text also lists water in the magneto distributor and carbon tracking, which make a spark reach the wrong plug; the FAA text says pre-ignition is caused by a hot spot, not by incorrect ignition timing, and this lesson follows the FAA definition.

mediaPlan.rationale: The 3D step that follows shows where such a hot spot can sit.

steps.title: Where a hot spot can sit
steps.prompt: At 340° the piston is rising on the compression stroke and is nearly at the top. Both valves are shut, and the charge is as hot and as squeezed as it will get before the spark. Anything in this chamber that is glowing, an eroded or cracked piston crown, the edge of a burned exhaust valve, a broken plug insulator, or a flake of deposit, can light the charge early. Spotlit here are the piston crown, the exhaust valve and the spark plugs.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 398 (a cracked valve or piston, or a broken spark plug insulator, may furnish a hot point that serves as a glow plug; deposits on the chamber surfaces from leaded fuels, and normal carbon deposits, can cause pre-ignition) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 44 (an exhaust valve that leaks and overheats can become incandescent at its edge and ignite the charge during compression). The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The compression-stroke pose with the surfaces that can glow spotlit shows where a hot spot can sit.

steps.title: Detonation or pre-ignition?
steps.prompt: They are easy to mix up, and one can start the other. Ask when and why. Pre-ignition begins before the spark, because something hot lights the charge early. Detonation begins after the spark, because the last of the charge cannot stand the heat and pressure. Pre-ignition is a hot spot and needs a cooler cylinder; detonation is a limit passed and needs less power, a richer mixture or a higher grade of fuel. Early spark timing is neither a hot spot nor detonation, but it can bring on detonation. Try to say which one you would suspect for each of these: a hole burned through a piston, a sudden rise in head temperature with roughness, a dished piston found at overhaul.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 398 (detonation often leads to pre-ignition; pre-ignition is a condition similar to early timing of the spark, but it is caused by a hot spot in the combustion chamber, not by incorrect ignition timing) and PDF p. 396 (early ignition can cause detonation). The contrast and the prompt are this lesson's comparison of those definitions.

mediaPlan.rationale: A comparison prompt that makes the learner state the two definitions in their own words.

steps.title: Backfiring
steps.prompt: A mixture that is far too lean burns slowly, so slowly that it is still burning when the exhaust stroke ends. The flame lingers, and when the intake valve opens it lights the charge in the induction system. That bang is a backfire, and it can damage the carburettor and the other induction parts. Wrong ignition timing or faulty ignition wires can do it too, by firing a cylinder when the intake valve is open. Backfiring rarely involves the whole engine, so it is seldom the carburettor's fault: it is usually one or two cylinders running leaner than the rest, from wrong valve clearance or a bad injector nozzle. If it happens only at idle, suspect an idle mixture that is too lean.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 398 (an extremely lean mixture burns so slowly that combustion is not complete at the end of the exhaust stroke; the flame ignites the contents of the induction system when the intake valve opens, which is backfiring and can damage the carburetor and induction parts; incorrect timing or faulty ignition wires can cause the cylinder to fire while the intake valve is open; backfiring rarely involves the whole engine, is limited to one or two cylinders, and usually results from faulty valve clearance or defective injector nozzles; backfiring in the idle range only is most likely an excessively lean idle mixture) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 44 (backfire results from slow burning of the lean mixture; the flame travels back through the combustible mixture in the induction system). The daily quiz also asks that an excessively lean mixture at high power can cause overheating, backfiring through the intake and a risk of detonation.

mediaPlan.rationale: Text only: the cause and the usual place are what the learner has to know.

steps.title: Afterfiring
steps.prompt: Backfiring is a fire in the intake; afterfiring is a fire in the exhaust. An overly rich mixture burns slowly too, so unburned fuel is left in the exhaust gas. When it meets air from outside the stack, it ignites with a bang. Long exhaust ducting makes it more likely. A cylinder that is not firing can do the same thing: a faulty plug, a defective injector nozzle or wrong valve clearance lets raw mixture pass into the exhaust, where it burns. That torching can be mistaken for a rich carburettor, so the cure is to find the real cause. The cold cylinder check, shown later in this lesson, finds dead or intermittent cylinders.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 399 (afterfiring, or afterburning, often results from a mixture that is too rich; unburned fuel in the exhaust gases mixes with air from outside the stacks and ignites in the exhaust system; more common with long exhaust ducting; it can also be caused by cylinders that are not firing, because of faulty plugs, defective fuel-injection nozzles or incorrect valve clearance, and can be mistaken for a rich carburetor; dead or intermittent cylinders can be located by the cold cylinder check) and PDF p. 404 (a mixture that is too rich is indicated by sluggish operation, a red exhaust flame and black smoke).

mediaPlan.rationale: A contrast with backfiring: same slow burning, different place and opposite mixture.

steps.title: Blow-by
steps.prompt: Blow-by is compression escaping from a cylinder past something that should have sealed it. Some gas always passes the piston ring gaps and is why the crankcase is vented. Too much means worn rings, a lack of oil or a valve that does not seat. Valve blow-by shows as a hiss or whistle when you pull the propeller through, turn the engine with the starter or, with an intake valve, hear it through the carburettor. Fix it at once, to save the valve and the engine: run a compression test, check the valve clearance, and free a sticking valve with a fibre drift. The next most common cause of low compression is leakage past the piston.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 407 (valve blow-by is a hissing or whistle when pulling the propeller through, turning with the starter, or heard through the carburetor when the intake valve leaks; correct it immediately by a compression test, then checking valve clearance and freeing a sticking valve with a fiber drift on the rocker arm; if blow-by remains, the cylinder may need replacing) and PDF p. 409 (next to valve blow-by, the most frequent cause of compression leakage is leakage past the piston, which can be due to lack of oil), with EASA Module 16, PDF p. 233 (the crankcase vent relieves the pressure that builds up from combustion blow-by seeping past the piston ring end gaps). The course deck (slide 254) adds that ring gaps aligned at assembly cause severe blow-by.

mediaPlan.rationale: The 3D step on where compression leaks in the Factors Affecting Power lesson already shows the leak paths.

steps.title: Reading the magneto check
steps.prompt: At the run-up you switch from both magnetos to one, and the engine drops a little in rpm because half the plugs are not firing. How it drops tells you where to look. A fast drop, the instant you switch, points to a faulty plug or ignition lead, because the cylinder goes dead at once. A slow drop points to late ignition timing or wrong valve clearance. No drop at all, or an engine that does not cut out with the switch off, means a faulty ground connection, and that is a safety problem. Complete cutting out on one magneto means that side is dead. Give each position time to settle, and tap the tachometer.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 394-395 (the magneto safety check; a slight but noticeable drop shows the opposite magneto is properly grounded out; failure to get any drop, or failure to cut out in the off position, means a faulty ground connection and a safety problem; a fast drop is usually from faulty plugs or harness; a slow drop is usually from incorrect timing or faulty valve adjustment; complete cutting out is definite evidence that side is not working; allow time to settle, up to a minute on one magneto is not excessive; a sticking tachometer can hide the true drop) and the daily quiz (day 6-7: the magneto check confirms each magneto circuit works and the drop is within limits). The permitted drop is the manufacturer's figure and is not given here.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner has to hold the pattern in mind; a table in the check below tests it.

steps.title: Power and cold cylinder checks
steps.prompt: With the propeller at low pitch, a good engine needs a known manifold pressure to turn a given rpm. A dead cylinder makes the others work harder, so manifold pressure rises: higher than normal means a dead cylinder or late timing, and lower than normal means early timing. To find the cylinder, run the engine on its roughest magneto, stop it with the mixture control, then read each head with a cold cylinder indicator. Only the pattern matters. In one example, on the right magneto cylinders 5 and 6 read 70 and 60 where cylinders 1 and 2 read 180 and 170, and cylinder 6 was also cold on the left magneto.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 396 (a higher than normal manifold pressure usually indicates a dead cylinder or late ignition timing; an excessively low manifold pressure usually indicates early timing; identical engines should need the same manifold pressure to within 1 inHg), PDF p. 406 (an engine that needs 32 inHg for 2,200 rpm where it used to need 30 has a likely cylinder malfunction) and PDF pp. 411-412 (the cold cylinder check, with the readings of Figure 10-56: right magneto cylinders 3, 5 and 6 cool or cold, left magneto cylinders 4 and 6 cold, cylinder 6 completely dead; the temperatures are relative and an ignition check alone would not disclose cylinder 6; the causes of a dead cylinder include defective plugs, wrong valve clearance, leaking intake pipes, lack of compression, a defective lead and a defective injector nozzle).

mediaPlan.rationale: The two checks are explained in words and the example readings are in the check below.

steps.title: Diagnose a squawk
steps.prompt: You are the technician. At a run-up at 1,700 rpm the pilot reports: both magnetos give a normal drop of about 60 rpm, but on the right one the drop is 300 rpm and the engine runs very roughly. Say what you think is wrong and why, using the fast and slow drop rule. Then say what you would check first and what test you would use to find the cylinder. Finish by naming one malfunction from this lesson that this fault could lead to if it were left, and why.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner applies the magneto check and cold cylinder check (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence). The squawk is from the course deck (slide 277, squawk A: a 60 rpm drop on the left, a 300 rpm drop and violent roughness on the right, deduced to be a defective spark plug or open ignition lead on the right magneto circuit), read with FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 394-395 (a fast drop is usually a faulty plug or harness) and PDF pp. 411-412 (the cold cylinder check).

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner works the diagnosis in their own words; the deck gives the squawk.

checks.question: Match each general requirement to what it asks of the engine.
checks.hint: Each requirement answers a different question.

pairs.right: A low weight for each horsepower it develops
A low fuel flow for each horsepower, measured as specific fuel consumption
A long time between failures, at rated power in any attitude and weather
Smooth running and the wanted performance from idle to full power

checks.rationale: The handbook measures durability by the mean time between overhauls and reliability by the mean time between failures; specific weight is weight per brake horsepower; specific fuel consumption is fuel flow per brake horsepower.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H develops 375 horsepower and has a standard dry weight of 550.39 lb. What is its specific weight, to two decimal places?
checks.hint: Specific weight is the engine's weight per brake horsepower.
checks.rationale: 550.39 ÷ 375 = 1.468, which is 1.47 lb per horsepower. Lower is better because every extra pound reduces the aircraft's performance.

checks.question: An engine burns 150 lb of fuel an hour while developing 300 brake horsepower. What is its brake-specific fuel consumption?
checks.hint: Fuel flow in lb/hr divided by brake horsepower.
checks.rationale: 150 ÷ 300 = 0.5 lb of fuel per hour for each brake horsepower. A lower figure means better fuel economy.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H develops its rated 375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm, and its propeller drive ratio is 0.667:1. At what crankshaft speed does it do so? Give the nearest whole number.
checks.hint: The propeller turns at 0.667 of the crankshaft speed.
checks.rationale: Crankshaft speed = propeller speed ÷ drive ratio = 2275 ÷ 0.667 = 3,411 rpm. The reduction gear lets the engine run fast while the propeller turns slowly enough to be efficient.

checks.question: A six-cylinder four-stroke engine completes its cycle in 720° of crankshaft rotation. How many degrees of rotation are there between one cylinder firing and the next?
checks.hint: Six firings are spread evenly over the whole cycle.
checks.rationale: 720° ÷ 6 cylinders = 120° between firings, which keeps the power pulses even. The GTSIO-520-H fires 1-4-5-2-3-6.

checks.question: For an aircraft that cruises at no more than about 250 mph, which type of engine is usually chosen?
checks.hint: Think about efficiency and cost at low speed.
answers: A reciprocating engine, for its efficiency and low cost
A turbofan, for its high-speed efficiency
A pure turbojet with afterburning
checks.rationale: The handbook says the reciprocating engine is the usual choice up to 250 mph because of its excellent efficiency and relatively low cost at low speed.

checks.question: Who recommends the time between overhauls (TBO) for an engine?
checks.hint: The engine's rating does not fix it.
answers: The engine manufacturer
The pilot at each flight
The airport where the aircraft is based
checks.rationale: Recommended TBOs are specified by the engine manufacturer. The actual interval varies with the operating conditions, the time at high power and the maintenance given.

checks.question: Why does an engine need to be compact?
checks.hint: There are several reasons.
answers: It streamlines and balances the aircraft better, improves the pilot's view and reduces drag
It lets the engine run at a higher compression ratio
It makes the fuel burn more slowly
checks.rationale: A small, well-shaped engine helps streamlining and balancing, gives a single-engine pilot a better view and creates less drag. It also makes it easier to keep the specific weight within limits.

checks.question: According to the GTSIO-520-H data page, when does the spark occur?
checks.hint: Look at the second specification page.
answers: 20 degrees before top centre, on both magnetos
20 degrees after top centre, on one magneto
At top centre, on both magnetos
checks.rationale: Page C-3-3 lists the spark at 20° BTC on both magnetos. A general handbook gives a range of 20° to 35° across engines; the manufacturer's value is the one that applies.

checks.question: The data page gives the maximum metered fuel pressure at "39.5 inches of mercury manifold pressure and 2275 propeller rpm". Why does it say that?
checks.hint: Think about what changes with power setting.
answers: A figure only means something with the conditions it is quoted for
Because the pressure never changes with power
Because the pressure is measured only in flight
checks.rationale: Fuel pressure depends on the power setting, so the data gives the manifold pressure and propeller speed at which the limit applies. Reading a number without its condition leads to mistakes.

checks.question: Match each malfunction to what happens in the cylinder or the engine.
checks.hint: Think about when the burning starts, and where.

pairs.right: The unburned charge explodes after the spark, ahead of the flame
A hot spot lights the charge before the spark
A lean charge still burning lights the mixture in the intake
Unburned fuel ignites in the exhaust system
Compression leaks past the rings or a valve

checks.rationale: Detonation and pre-ignition are both early or violent burning in the chamber, but detonation follows the spark and pre-ignition comes before it. Backfiring and afterfiring are fires outside the cylinder, in the intake and in the exhaust. Blow-by is a leak, not a fire.

checks.question: Match each run-up sign to its likely cause.
checks.hint: A fault in a plug or a lead takes effect at once; a timing fault does not.

pairs.left: A fast rpm drop on one magneto
pairs.right: A faulty spark plug or ignition lead

pairs.left: A slow rpm drop on one magneto
pairs.right: Late ignition timing or wrong valve clearance

pairs.left: No rpm drop on one magneto
pairs.right: A faulty ground connection on one side

pairs.left: Engine cuts out on one magneto
pairs.right: That magneto's side of the ignition is dead

pairs.left: Higher manifold pressure than normal for the rpm
pairs.right: A dead cylinder or late ignition timing

checks.rationale: A faulty plug or lead makes its cylinder go dead the instant the switch moves, so the drop is fast. A timing or valve fault lowers the peak pressure and the drop comes on slowly. No drop means the other magneto is not being grounded out, which is a safety fault.

checks.question: Which statement correctly separates pre-ignition from detonation?
checks.hint: One of them starts before the spark.
answers: Pre-ignition is caused by spark timing that is too early; detonation is caused by a hot spot
Pre-ignition starts before the timed spark, from a hot spot; detonation is the unburned charge exploding after the spark
They are two names for the same event
checks.rationale: The handbook is clear that pre-ignition is caused by a hot spot, not by incorrect ignition timing. Detonation is the spontaneous burning of the unburned charge after ignition. Detonation can lead to pre-ignition, but they are not the same.

checks.question: Why can light detonation continue through many takeoffs without the crew noticing?
checks.hint: Think about what the pilot would feel or see.
answers: Light to medium detonation gives no noticeable roughness, temperature rise or loss of power
It only happens when the engine is stopped
The engine shuts down at once, so there is nothing to notice
checks.rationale: Light to medium detonation gives no flight deck evidence. Its effects are usually discovered at teardown: dished piston heads, collapsed valve heads, broken ring lands or eroded valves and pistons.

checks.question: Pre-ignition shows up at high power, with roughness and a sudden rise in head temperature. What is the immediate action?
checks.hint: The aim is to cool the cylinder.
answers: Lean the mixture to burn less fuel
Open the throttle to blow out the deposits
Retard the throttle, and enrich the mixture if possible
checks.rationale: Retarding the throttle reduces the fuel charge and the heat. Enriching the mixture then cools the combustion. Retarding the throttle for a few seconds can even chip off a deposit that is acting as a hot spot.

checks.question: One cylinder keeps backfiring through the induction system while the others run smoothly. What is the most likely cause?
checks.hint: Backfiring rarely involves the whole engine.
answers: That cylinder runs leaner than the rest, for example from valve clearance or a defective injector nozzle
The carburettor is out of adjustment for the whole engine
The mixture is too rich in all cylinders
checks.rationale: Backfiring is almost always limited to one or two cylinders that run leaner than the engine as a whole, and the handbook points to valve clearance and injector nozzles. It is seldom the fault of the carburettor.

checks.question: Flames appear in the exhaust. What other fault than a rich mixture can cause this?
checks.hint: Where does the mixture from a cylinder that is not firing go?
answers: A leak in the oil cooler
A dead or intermittently firing cylinder passing unburned mixture into the exhaust
Too much oil in the sump
checks.rationale: The unburned mixture from a cylinder that is not firing, because of a faulty plug, a bad injector nozzle or wrong valve clearance, passes into the exhaust, mixes with air and burns. It can look like a rich carburettor.

checks.question: During a compression test on one cylinder, air is heard escaping at the crankcase breather. Where is it leaking past?
checks.hint: Air from the breather has come into the crankcase.
answers: The intake valve
The exhaust valve
The piston and rings
checks.rationale: Air escaping at the breather has passed the piston into the crankcase. A leak past the exhaust valve is heard at the exhaust outlet, and one past the intake valve at the air intake.

checks.question: Which set of signs points to a mixture that is too rich?
checks.hint: Rich gives a cool, sluggish burn with unburned fuel.
answers: Overheating and backfiring
Sluggish running, a red exhaust flame and black smoke
Detonation damage at teardown
checks.rationale: The handbook's troubleshooting chart gives sluggish operation, a red exhaust flame and black smoke for a mixture that is too rich, and overheating or backfiring for one that is too lean.

checks.question: A cold cylinder check on a six-cylinder engine gives these relative readings for cylinders 1 to 6. Right magneto: 180, 170, 100, 145, 70, 60. Left magneto: 170, 175, 170, 60, 155, 45. Which cylinder is dead on both magnetos?
checks.hint: Look for the one reading very low in both rows.
checks.rationale: Cylinder 6 reads 60 on the right and 45 on the left, far below the others in both rows. Cylinder 5 is cold only on the right and cylinder 4 only on the left. An ignition check alone would not find cylinder 6, because it is dead on both switch positions.

checks.question: Put the steps of a cold cylinder check in order.
checks.hint: The cylinders must be read before they cool, so the order follows the engine stopping.
items: Run the engine on its roughest magneto at 1,200 to 1,600 rpm until the head temperature is steady
Stop it with the mixture control at idle cutoff or full lean
Switch off both the ignition and the master switch when it stops firing
Apply the cold cylinder indicator to each cylinder in order, firmly and at the same spot
Compare the readings to find the dead or intermittent cylinders
checks.rationale: The engine is run until the temperatures are stable, then stopped, then the indicator is applied as quickly as possible once the propeller has stopped. The readings only mean something when compared with the other cylinders on the same engine.
